title: Energy-Efficient Houses: Orientation, Shading and Rooftop Solar
desc: How to design a cool, low-electricity home: orientation, shading the west side, roof insulation, windows, ventilation and points to note on rooftop solar.
summary: Architectural solutions that reduce heat and save electricity in houses: orientation, shading, roof insulation, natural ventilation, appliances and rooftop solar.
body: p

For many families, summer electricity bills come mainly from air conditioning. Most of the heat enters the house through the roof and the west-facing walls. Getting the design right from the start keeps the house cooler without much extra cost; appliances and solar power are only an additional step.
h2
1. House orientation and room layout
ul
In Vietnam, a house facing south or southeast usually catches cool summer breezes and little harsh sun; a west face takes the hottest afternoon sun.
For a townhouse where you cannot choose the orientation, arrange rooms smartly: place the staircase, storage and bathrooms on the west side as a “buffer layer”, and bedrooms on the cooler side.
Open doors on two opposite sides for cross-ventilation; combine with a light well so hot air escapes upward.
h2
2. Shade before the sun enters the house
ul

Overhangs, sun-shading louvres and eaves over west- and south-facing windows. Shading from the outside works better than indoor curtains because the heat is blocked before it passes through the glass.
Deep balconies and loggias are both usable space and shade for the rooms behind.
Plants, climbing trellises on the west face and on the rooftop terrace help reduce radiant heat.
p

Balconies, louvres and overhangs projecting outward must comply with the detailed plan and the local architectural management regulations; where the house has a setback, the projecting part must not exceed the red line, and must not cross the plot boundary into the neighbouring house (sections 2.5.7 and 2.5.8 of QCVN 01:2026/BXD, effective from 1 January 2027). See also How architectural management regulations affect building a house.
h2
3. Insulating the roof and walls
ul

The roof receives the most sun. Commonly used solutions: a double roof with a ventilated gap, an insulation layer, heat-reflective paint, an insulated sheet-metal roof, a rooftop terrace with a cover or a roof garden (which needs waterproofing and a load calculation).
West-facing walls can be built as double walls, with insulating material or clad with louvres.
A light-coloured exterior finish absorbs less heat than a dark one.
h2
4. Windows and glass
p

Large glass doors give beautiful light but also let heat in. On the west face, limit the glass area, or use heat-reducing glass combined with external shading. Windows should be openable for ventilation when the weather is cool, not just fixed glass.
h2
5. Energy-saving appliances
ul
Inverter air conditioners, with a capacity suited to the room area; put the outdoor unit in an open place away from direct sun.
LED lamps, and daylighting through light wells and windows during the day.
A solar water heater or heat pump for larger households.
h2
6. Rooftop solar: what to note?
ul

Roof structure: panels and mounting frames add load and must resist storms and wind; an engineer should check the roof, especially an older house or a sheet-metal roof. Fixing points must be carefully sealed against leaks.
Orientation and shading: panels should be little shaded by taller neighbouring buildings, water tanks and trees.

Electrical safety and fire prevention: cables, switchboards and the inverter must be installed to proper technical standards, with protective devices; avoid putting the inverter in an enclosed, hot place.
Procedures: grid connection and selling surplus electricity (if any) follow the electricity sector's current rules – ask the local power company before installing.
Calculate the payback period based on the electricity the household uses in the daytime; do not install a system that is too large for your needs.
p
